strengths: The paper addresses a relevant phenomenon: strong clean generalization can coexist with near-perfect robust training accuracy and poor robust test accuracy.

Combining representation complexity with feature-learning dynamics is a worthwhile direction. The signal/noise decomposition provides an interpretable hypothesis for how partial signal learning and sample-specific memorization can coexist.

Experiments cover MNIST, CIFAR-10, synthetic data, and local-flatness diagnostics. The reported results illustrate the motivating phenomenon; for example, the largest CIFAR-10 model achieves 86.05% clean test accuracy, 99.57% robust training accuracy, and 50.08% robust test accuracy.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under its stated assumptions. Consider equiprobable inputs ±e₁ with matching labels, δ=1/4, and f_clean(x)=x₁−0.9. This satisfies Assumptions 4.1–4.3: clean error is zero and robust test error is 1/2. As the sample grows, both atoms have empirical frequencies near 1/2, so vanishing robust training error forces zero robust test error, making CGRO impossible. The theorem needs assumptions controlling support coverage. Additionally, class separation does not imply disjoint same-class training balls, and Appendix F incorrectly claims uniform o(1) approximation of a generally discontinuous indicator-based classifier by continuous ReLU networks.

Theorem 5.9 does not establish CGRO under the robustness definition in Section 3. Training attacks modify only the signal patch along w*, leaving the memorized noise untouched. Small adversarial loss over this restricted set does not imply small robust training error over the full perturbation ball. Appendix E.12 makes this unsupported implication, undermining a principal conclusion.

The dynamics proof contains additional substantive errors. Appendix E.2 absorbs the factor 1−λ into a positive constant even though Assumption 5.7 permits λ=1, invalidating the stated signal-growth argument for standard adversarial training. Appendix E.12 treats cubic Gaussian projections as sub-Gaussian, which they are not, and therefore does not justify the concentration bound used to establish clean generalization.

The supplementary generalization bound in Theorem B.1 is also unsupported as stated. A constant predictor can have zero input gradient but different losses on the two labels. Its empirical risk still fluctuates with sampled label proportions, whereas the proposed bound has an identically zero correction term and would require population risk to be below empirical risk with high probability. Smoothness of the input density does not resolve this counterexample.

The synthetic experiment does not satisfy the claimed theoretical setting: Section 6.2 uses δ=α=10, whereas Assumption 5.7 requires δ<α. At δ=α, an allowed attack can erase the entire signal, leaving noise independent of the label. Poor robust test performance is therefore unavoidable even for an optimal classifier and cannot validate the proposed optimization-induced explanation.

The real-data experiments provide qualitative associations rather than convincing evidence for the claimed mechanism. Capacity sweeps and flatness correlations do not distinguish representation limitations from optimization failure or establish that learned networks implement local memorization indicators. PGD iteration counts, step sizes, restarts, and variability across runs are not adequately reported, limiting reproducibility and confidence in the robustness measurements.

The novelty of the lower-bound extension over Li et al. (2022) is insufficiently explained. Although advertised as extending beyond linearly separable settings, Appendix F still constructs linearly separable data, and Theorem 4.7 is existential. A precise comparison of assumptions and conclusions is needed to establish what additional hardness result is obtained.
